148.text:
Genetically modified crops, whose genes have been altered in a laboratory to give them useful traits, are widely grown in some countries and banned in others. This essay will discuss the main advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, genetically modified crops can produce higher and more reliable yields. Plants can be changed to resist pests, tolerate drought or contain extra vitamins, so farmers lose less of their harvest and need fewer chemicals. More food is then grown on the same land, which helps a growing population. A farmer who plants a drought-resistant variety, for example, may still harvest a reasonable crop in a dry year, when ordinary seed would fail. Crops improved in this way can also reduce hunger and malnutrition in poorer regions.

On the negative side, however, the long-term effects of genetically modified crops are not fully known. Modified genes could spread to wild plants, and farmers who buy patented seed each year become dependent on a few large companies. Many consumers distrust modified food, and people in some countries worry about its safety even though the evidence so far is limited. Nevertheless, these concerns can be addressed. Careful testing, independent regulation and clear labels would allow consumers to make their own choices and would help to detect problems early.

In conclusion, genetically modified crops offer real benefits for food supply, but uncertainty about long-term effects and corporate control are valid concerns. On balance, I believe that they should be used cautiously, under strict testing and open information.

257.text:
Farming has changed more in the last few decades than in the previous thousand years, thanks to new machines, seeds and software. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on agricultural innovation: higher output with fewer resources, and stronger rural communities.

First and foremost, agricultural innovation allows farmers to produce more with fewer resources. Drip irrigation, sensors and better seeds deliver water and fertiliser exactly where plants need them, so yields rise while waste falls. A farm that switches from flooding its fields to drip irrigation, for example, can grow the same crop with far less water, which matters in dry regions. As a result, the country can feed its growing population without clearing more forest or farmland, and it saves money on chemicals and fuel. Drones and satellite images also help farmers to spot disease early and treat only the affected area.

In addition, innovation strengthens rural economies. Higher output and lower costs raise farm incomes, and new technology creates skilled jobs in areas such as equipment maintenance, data analysis and food processing. Young people who might otherwise leave for cities can find attractive careers in the countryside, which keeps villages alive. A country that develops advanced farming methods can also sell its equipment and expertise to others. Although new technology may be expensive for small farmers, shared equipment and training schemes can spread the benefits widely.

To sum up, agricultural innovation brings clear benefits to a country, above all greater and more efficient food production and a more prosperous countryside. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

295.text:
Agriculture is often seen as an old-fashioned sector, yet it remains the foundation of every economy. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on agriculture: food security and a stable rural economy.

First and foremost, a strong farming sector protects a country's food security. A country that grows its own food depends less on imports and is less exposed to sudden price rises or supply problems on the world market. Reliable harvests also keep food affordable for ordinary families, which reduces hunger and protects public health. Countries that support their farmers during bad years, for example, can avoid shortages and keep prices stable. A nation that relies heavily on imported grain, in contrast, can find itself in difficulty when exporters restrict sales.

In addition, agriculture supports employment and rural stability. Farming, food processing, transport and equipment sales provide jobs and income for millions of people, particularly in areas with few other industries. This helps rural communities to remain viable, so that fewer people move to crowded cities in search of work, which in turn eases pressure on housing and services. Agricultural exports also earn foreign currency that can pay for imports of machinery and medicine. Because food is always in demand, the sector is relatively stable even when other industries face difficulties. Although farming depends on weather and is vulnerable to climate change, modern methods and insurance can reduce the risks.

To sum up, focusing on agriculture brings clear benefits to a country, above all food security and a stable rural economy. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

327.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether urban farming can solve food shortages. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that urban farming brings fresh food closer to the people who eat it. Rooftop gardens, vertical farms and community plots use empty space in cities, cut transport distances and give residents access to fresh vegetables that would otherwise be expensive or hard to find. Local food costs less to deliver, loses less on the way and strengthens community ties, since neighbours work together and learn about growing. A block of flats that grows salad leaves on its roof, for example, can supply nearby households and restaurants throughout the year. In districts where fresh produce is scarce, this can improve diets and reduce hunger.

On the other hand, critics point out that urban farms cannot grow enough staple crops to end food shortages. Cities lack the land and water needed for wheat, rice and maize, which feed most of the world, and high rents and energy costs make indoor farms expensive. Most urban farms produce leafy vegetables and herbs, which are valuable but provide few calories. A large city that tried to feed itself from its own rooftops, for instance, would run out of space very quickly.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that urban farming is a useful supplement that improves access to fresh food, but it cannot replace rural agriculture or solve shortages on its own.

350.text:
Pesticides, which are chemicals used to kill insects, weeds and fungi, are applied to crops in almost every farming region. This essay will discuss the main advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, pesticides protect crops from insects, weeds and disease. Without them farmers could lose a large share of their harvest, which would raise food prices and leave more people hungry. They also allow fruit and vegetables to look attractive and to last longer in shops, so less food is thrown away. A grower whose orchard is hit by a destructive insect, for example, may lose most of the fruit within weeks unless the pest is controlled. For many families, cheaper and more reliable food is a real benefit.

On the negative side, however, pesticides can harm people, wildlife and water. Residues may stay on food, chemicals wash into rivers and kill useful insects such as bees, and pests gradually become resistant, which forces farmers to use stronger products. Farm workers who handle these chemicals without protection may also suffer from illness. Nevertheless, the harm can be reduced. Integrated pest management, which combines natural predators, crop rotation and small amounts of spraying only when needed, protects harvests while using far fewer chemicals. Strict rules on which products are allowed and on safe use would also help.

In conclusion, pesticides play an important role in feeding the world, but their effects on health and the environment are serious. On balance, I believe that they should be used sparingly and under strict control, alongside safer methods.

482.text:
Shoppers today buy food that has often travelled thousands of kilometres, and many of them have no idea where it was grown. I largely agree that food origin should be labelled on products, since labels help shoppers to make informed choices, although the rules should not be too costly.

To begin with, labels showing where food comes from help shoppers to make informed choices. Buyers can support local farmers, avoid products linked to poor safety records or very long transport, and decide whether they are willing to pay more for particular regions. If a problem such as contamination occurs, a clear origin also makes it easier to trace the source and withdraw the product quickly. A shopper who reads that apples were grown in a nearby region, for example, may choose them over apples flown from another continent, which reduces transport emissions.

Furthermore, labelling gives producers a reason to meet higher standards. When customers can see the origin, farmers and companies are more careful about quality and honesty, because their reputation is visible. It also protects consumers from misleading claims, such as a product described as local when only the packaging was done nearby. However, there are costs. Small producers may find complicated labelling expensive, and origin does not always indicate quality, since good and bad products exist in every country. Rules should therefore be simple and consistent, and phased in with support for small businesses.

In conclusion, food origin should be labelled to a large extent, because it improves choice and accountability, provided that the rules are clear and affordable.

486.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be spent on organic farming or on other priorities such as health and education. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of organic farming argue that it reduces chemical use and protects soil and wildlife. Organic farmers avoid synthetic pesticides and fertilisers, which keeps soil healthy, protects rivers from chemical runoff and supports insects, birds and other wildlife. Many consumers also prefer organic food and are willing to pay more for it, so public support can help farmers to enter a growing market. A farm that rotates crops and uses natural compost, for example, may improve its soil year after year while producing food with fewer chemical residues.

On the other hand, critics point out that governments have limited funds and many equally urgent responsibilities. Hospitals, schools, housing and welfare all need money now, and organic farming has drawbacks. Yields are usually lower, so more land is needed to produce the same amount of food, and organic products are often more expensive, which makes them hard to afford for poorer families. Spending large sums on one method of farming may therefore bring little benefit compared with spending on public services. A town with overcrowded classrooms, for instance, has more pressing needs than a grant for organic growers.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that other priorities should receive most of the budget, with modest and targeted support for sustainable farming where the environmental benefits are clear.

analysis.type_vi: Discuss both views: chi tiêu chính phủ cho nông nghiệp hữu cơ hay ưu tiên khác

plan.think: Dùng lại cấu trúc 'limited funds / equally urgent' của đề 498 và 31 cho phe 'ưu tiên khác'.
Ít thuốc trừ sâu và phân hoá học nên đất khoẻ, sông ít bị ô nhiễm, động vật hoang dã được bảo vệ; người tiêu dùng sẵn sàng trả nhiều hơn. Ví dụ trang trại luân canh và dùng phân hữu cơ.
Ngân sách có hạn nên y tế, trường học, nhà ở cần tiền ngay; hữu cơ năng suất thấp, cần nhiều đất, giá cao khó với gia đình nghèo. Ví dụ thị trấn lớp học quá đông.
Phần lớn ngân sách cho ưu tiên khác, hỗ trợ có mục tiêu cho nông nghiệp bền vững khi lợi ích môi trường rõ ràng.

399.text:
Hundreds of millions of people still lack a safe and reliable water supply. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on clean water access: better health and wider opportunities for education and work.

First and foremost, clean water protects health. Safe drinking water prevents diseases such as diarrhoea and cholera, which kill many young children, and proper sanitation stops infections from spreading. As a result, fewer people become ill, hospitals are less crowded and families spend less on medicine. A village that gains a safe tap, for example, sees fewer children miss school because of stomach illness, and healthier adults are able to work more regularly. In the long term, a healthy population is also cheaper for the country to support.

In addition, clean water frees time for education and work. Where there is no tap nearby, women and girls often spend several hours every day carrying water, which stops them from attending school or earning money. Piped water removes this burden, so more girls can complete their education and more adults can take paid jobs. Reliable water also supports farming, food processing and manufacturing, which raises productivity and attracts investment. Healthier, better-educated people make the economy stronger, and the benefits continue across generations. Although building pipes and treatment plants requires large investment, studies in many countries suggest that the returns in health and productivity are far greater than the cost.

To sum up, clean water access brings clear benefits to a country, above all better health and wider opportunities. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.
